title: Unpaid, not unvalued
hookLine: caring, housework and volunteering are work, and traditions honor them
carry: I saw what you did, and it mattered

cards: Who washed the dishes after dinner last night? Who sat up with the feverish child, drove the grandparent to the appointment, folded the laundry, coached the team, made the casserole for the neighbor after the funeral?
None of it shows up on a paycheck. When someone asks, so what do you do, almost none of it gets mentioned. And yet a household, a street, a congregation would start to fall apart without it.

teach.b: First, a name for it. Unpaid work is still work. Caring for children or the sick, keeping a home running, volunteering: they take time, skill and energy, just like paid jobs.
Only the money is missing, and money is not the only measure of worth. Second, a very old portrait. The last chapter of the book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, praises a capable woman.
Much of what it honors is the work of a household: she rises while it's still night, provides food, makes cloth, opens her hand to the poor.

One verse says, "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." In some Jewish homes, this poem is sung at the Friday night table. Housework, in that text, isn't invisible.
Third, a word from Sikh tradition: seva, selfless service. At a gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, volunteers cook and serve langar, a free communal meal open to anyone who walks in.
Others wash the dishes, sweep the floors, or care for visitors' shoes. Nobody is paid.
In Sikh teaching, this is not a lesser task than worship; seva is itself a way of serving God and the community, and anyone may take part, whatever their standing.
Fourth, what this asks of us.
If unpaid work is real work, then the people doing it deserve real thanks. Not a vague nod at holidays, but a specific word: I saw what you did, and it mattered.

how: Sikhs perform seva at gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, cleaning and caring for visitors; in some Jewish homes the poem from Proverbs 31 is sung at the Friday night table.

games.q: you walk into a gurdwara at mealtime. you're a stranger and not a Sikh. what happens?
o: you're asked to pay for the meal.
you're welcome to sit and eat langar.
games.why: langar is a free communal meal open to anyone, cooked and served by volunteers as seva.

practice: Bring to mind a meal someone cooked for you, a bed someone made, a hard day someone sat through with you, and let one person stand out, their hands doing the work.
Then let your own unpaid work come to mind too, the things nobody counts, and hold both without a ledger. If you pray, you can hold that person in your tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Unpaid. Work done without wages, caring, housework, volunteering, that is still real work, and honored in the old texts and traditions. Today's word.
